title: Hisatake Ishida
text:
Coral hologenome data, generated by sequencing DNA from whole coral tissue, are dominated by host sequences, and the remaining 5 to 10% of reads are often discarded as “contaminant”. We showed that this fraction is a goldmine: a PCR-free window into the endosymbiotic dinoflagellates (Symbiodiniaceae) living in hospite. We reviewed assembly-based, read alignment-based and alignment-free (k-mer) approaches, and using 148 hologenomes of Acropora kenti from the central Great Barrier Reef, resolved symbiont communities that track riverine influence. The workflow, Symb-SHIN, now scales to thousands of hologenomes.
Published in Frontiers in Eukaryotic Microbiology

title: Hisatake Ishida
section: Diversity and metabolism of Great Barrier Reef sediment microbes
text:
Diversity and metabolism of Great Barrier Reef sediment microbes


Reef sediments are a hotspot of nutrient cycling, yet their microbes remain largely unexplored at genome level. From 191 sediment metagenomes collected at 48 sites along the Great Barrier Reef, we recovered 2,698 metagenome-assembled genomes representing 1,201 species, 98% of which have no species-level representative in reference databases. Compared with co-located seawater, sediment microbes have larger, GC-rich genomes and greater metabolic versatility, including anaerobic respiration, nitrogen fixation, hydrogen metabolism and novel biosynthetic gene clusters.
Preprint on bioRxiv

title: Hisatake Ishida
text:
Senior research technician · Australian Centre for Ecogenomics, The University of Queensland


Hi, I am Take

I am a microbial genomicist at the Australian Centre for Ecogenomics, The University of Queensland. My research uses metagenomics, hologenomics, population genomics and phylogenomics to study the “challenging” microbes of coral reefs: the endosymbiotic dinoflagellates (family Symbiodiniaceae) living inside reef-building corals, and the free-living prokaryotes and viruses in reef sediments of the Great Barrier Reef.
During my PhD, supervised by Associate Professor Cheong Xin Chan and Professor Cynthia Riginos, I assessed Symbiodiniaceae communities in more than 4,000 coral hologenomes, recovered symbiont genomes directly from coral tissue, and built the first genome-resolved catalogue of Great Barrier Reef sediment microbes. I am interested in how microbial diversity, niche breadth and genome evolution underpin reef function, and in building microbial baselines that support reef monitoring and restoration.
I now maintain the Symbiodiniaceae living culture collection at ACE and develop software tools for teaching in undergraduate courses at UQ, while finalising manuscripts from my PhD. I am always happy to discuss potential collaborations, so please feel free to reach out!
